⚽ Most people looking at the FIFA World Cup focus on one question:

Who will win?

Bybit is taking a completely different approach with its new WC26 Goal Difference Futures.

Instead of simply predicting a winner, traders can speculate on the expected goal difference between the home team and away team.

This is important because the contract price is linked to expected net goals, not winning probability.

For example:

🏟 Home team wins 2-1
Goal Difference = +1
Settlement Price = 11

🏟 Match ends 1-1
Goal Difference = 0
Settlement Price = 10

🏟 Home team loses 1-2
Goal Difference = -1
Settlement Price = 9

The settlement formula is:

Settlement Price = 10 + Goal Difference

One thing many traders misunderstand is that a contract trading at 10.9 DOES NOT mean the team has a 90% chance of winning.

Instead, the market is pricing an expected goal difference of approximately +0.9 goals for the home side.

Another interesting feature is that these contracts remain tradable before and during the match. You can enter a position before kickoff, react to goals, red cards, injuries, substitutions, and changing momentum throughout the game.

Unlike traditional football betting, this is structured as a derivatives product where traders can:

✅ Go Long
✅ Go Short
✅ Use Limit Orders
✅ Set Take Profit
✅ Set Stop Loss
✅ Trade with up to 5x leverage

Bybit also confirmed there are NO funding fees on these contracts.

📰 GOP Lovebomb: When ‘No New Wars’ Meets No New Spine

Trump’s Iran deal didn’t just “end” a war, it cracked his own party open on live TV. The same Republicans who cheered him into Tehran now can’t decide what offends them more: the price tag, the optics, or the fact that Iran is still standing.

Senator Bill Cassidy, already politically executed by a Trump-backed primary challenger, says the Iran war was “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades” and that Tehran learned it can squeeze the Strait of Hormuz for concessions. 

Reagan, he declares, is “rolling over in his grave.” For a party that’s been worshipping Reagan’s ghost for forty years, that’s basically a fatwa.

On the other flank, MAGA isolationists are still stuck on the trailer: Trump promised “no new wars,” then launched one, then walked out with a deal that punts the nuclear question into a 60‑day “we’ll talk later” window and dangles a 300 billion dollar reconstruction fantasy over Iran. 

Hawks say it’s appeasement. Doves say it’s betrayal. Trump says it’s “historic.” Everyone else says: check the gas price.

The New York Post — not exactly a Berkeley faculty lounge — splashes a front page screaming that Trump “devastated Iran, now he hits them with a… LOVEBOMB,” accusing him of showering Tehran with cash and lifting sanctions. 

When you’ve lost your favorite tabloid, you haven’t made peace, you’ve triggered a shareholder revolt in the outrage business.

So the president does what he always does: he attacks his own base. Critics of the deal are “stupid and bad people,” ex‑friends are publicly downgraded in front of cameras, and anyone who questions the fine print is accused of wanting endless war just to feel tough.

The movement that sold itself as “America First” now looks like a circular firing squad arguing over whether the problem is too much war, too little war, or too little respect for Trump while the war was happening.

In the end, the Iran deal isn’t about Iran. It’s about a party that can’t admit the obvious: their strongman president started a war he couldn’t finish on his own terms, then signed a messy exit he can only defend by turning his own coalition into the enemy. 

Tehran gets time. Voters get higher prices. Trump gets another episode of his personal reality show, subtitled: 
“This Is What Winning Looks Like.”
